label: prop:wz
title: Proposition
body_md:
The functions in \eqref{eq:pair} form a meromorphic WZ pair.
\label{prop:wz}
head: environment

label: eq:n-ratio
title: Proof
head: environment

label: thm: parameter
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have
\begin{align*}
 &U(n,k)=4^{-n}\frac{(1/2)_n(1/2+2k)_n}{(1)_n(1+k)_n}
                   \frac{(1/4)_k(3/4)_k}{(1)_k^2}\\
F(n,k)&=-\frac{n}{2(n+k)}U(n,k),\
 G(n,k)=\frac{k(6n+4k+1)}{2(n+k)(2n+1)}U(n,k).         
 \end{align*}
as a WZ pair and $F(0,k)=0$ is trivial. First, we will prove $F(n,k)\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$.

For $k>0$, we have
\[
0<\frac{(1/2+2k)_n}{(1+k)_n}=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{2k+j+1/2}{k+j+1}\leq 2^n.
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Unk estimate}
  0<U(n,k)\leq \dfrac{(1/4)_k(3/4)_k}{(1)_k^2}\dfrac{(1/2)_n}{(1)_n}2^{-n}=\dfrac{(1/4)_k(3/4)_k}{(1)_k^2}\binom{2n}{n}8^{-n}.
\end{equation}
Then
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}F(n,k)=0.
\]

Summing the WZ relation over $n\ge 0$, we obtain
\[
 \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}G(n,k+1)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}G(n,k).
\]
To determine its value, fix $k_0>0$. By the Gamma-ratio asymptotic $\frac{\Gamma(z+a)}{\Gamma(z+b)}\sim z^{a-b}$ as $z\rightarrow\infty$ (see \cite[Formula 5.11.12]{DLMF}),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C(k)estimate}
  k\frac{(1/4)_k(3/4)_k}{(1)_k^2}=k\frac{1}{\Gamma(1/4)\Gamma(3/4)}\frac{\Gamma(k+1/4)}{\Gamma(k+1)}\frac{\Gamma(k+3/4)}{\Gamma(k+1)}\longrightarrow
\frac{1}{\Gamma(1/4)\Gamma(3/4)}
=
\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{2}}
\ (k\to\infty),
\end{equation}
and so it is bounded for $k\ge k_0$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:6n/n estimate}
  \frac{6n+4k+1}{n+k}\le 6+\frac{1}{k_0}.
\end{equation}
Followed by \eqref{eq:Unk estimate},\eqref{eq:C(k)estimate} and \eqref{eq:6n/n estimate}, we have
\[
0\le G(n,k)\leq C_{k_0}
\dfrac{\binom{2n}{n}8^{-n}}{2n+1},\quad\mbox{where  } C_{k_0}\ \mathrm{is\ a\ constant\ only\  about}\ k_0
\]
and the majorant on the right is summable. Hence the dominated convergence applies.

For fixed $n$, as $k\rightarrow\infty$,
\[
\frac{(1/2+2k)_n}{(1+k)_n}\longrightarrow 2^n,\ k\dfrac{(1/4)_k(3/4)_k}{(1)_k^2}\longrightarrow \dfrac{1}{\pi\sqrt{2}},\ \frac{6n+4k+1}{n+k}\longrightarrow 4
\]
and consequently
\[
G(n,k)\longrightarrow
\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\pi}
\dfrac{\binom{2n}{n}8^{-n}}{2n+1}.
\]
Since $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}G(n,k+1)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}G(n,k)$ for every integer $j\ge 0$, letting
$j\to\infty$ gives
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}G(n,k)=
\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\pi}
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
\dfrac{\binom{2n}{n}8^{-n}}{2n+1}.
\]
Using
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\binom{2n}{n}4^{-n}t^{2n}}{2n+1}
=
\frac{\arcsin t}{t},
\]
and taking $t=1/\sqrt{2}$, we obtain
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}G(n,k)=\frac12.
\]

On the other hand, from the definition of $G(n,k)$,
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}G(n,k)
=
\frac{k(1/4)_k(3/4)_k}{2(1)_k^2}
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
\frac{6n+4k+1}{(2n+1)(n+k)}
\frac{(1/2)_n(1/2+2k)_n}
{(1)_n(1+k)_n}
4^{-n}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
\frac{6n+4k+1}{(2n+1)(n+k)}
\frac{(1/2)_n(1/2+2k)_n}
{(1)_n(1+k)_n}
4^{-n}
=
\dfrac{(1)_k^2}{k(1/4)_k(3/4)_k}=4^k\sqrt{\pi}
\frac{\Gamma(k)\Gamma(k+1)}
{\Gamma(2k+1/2)}.
\]
and relabeling $k$ as $x$ proves the theorem.

label: coro:3log2
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first consider the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:parameter}. The term corresponding
to $n=0$ is
\[
\frac{4x+1}{x}=\frac1x+4.
\]
For $n\ge 1$, as $x\to 0^+$,
\[
\frac{6n+4x+1}{(2n+1)(n+x)}\frac{(1/2)_n(1/2+2x)_n}{(1)_n(1+x)_n}4^{-n}\longrightarrow\frac{6n+1}{n(2n+1)}\,c_n^2\,4^{-n},
\]
where $c_n=\frac{(1/2)_n}{(1)_n}=4^{-n}\binom{2n}{n}$.

Moreover, for $0\le x\le 1$, 
\[
\dfrac{6n+4x+1}{n+x}\le 7\quad \mathrm{and}\quad \dfrac{(1/2+2x)_n}{(1+x)_n}=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}
\frac{2x+j+1/2}{x+j+1}\le 2^n
\] 
then
\[
\left|
\frac{6n+4x+1}{(2n+1)(n+x)}
\frac{(1/2)_n(1/2+2x)_n}{(1)_n(1+x)_n}
4^{-n}
\right|
\le
\frac{7c_n2^{-n}}{2n+1}.
\]
Dominated convergence gives
\[
\lim_{x\to0^+}
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\frac{6n+4x+1}{(2n+1)(n+x)}
\frac{(1/2)_n(1/2+2x)_n}{(1)_n(1+x)_n}
4^{-n}
=
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\frac{6n+1}{n(2n+1)}c_n^2\,4^{-n}.
\]
Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rhs 3log2}
  \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
\frac{6n+4x+1}{(2n+1)(n+x)}
\frac{(1/2)_n(1/2+2x)_n}{(1)_n(1+x)_n}
4^{-n}
=
\frac1x+4
+
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\frac{6n+1}{n(2n+1)}c_n^2\,4^{-n}
+o(1)
\end{equation}
as $x\to0^+$.

For the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:parameter}, set
\[
A(x):=\frac{4^x\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(x)\Gamma(x+1)}{\Gamma(2x+1/2)}\ \mathrm{and}\ B(x):=xA(x)=\frac{4^x\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(x+1)^2}
{\Gamma(2x+1/2)}.
\]
Then $B(x)$ is regular at $x=0$, and $B(0)=1$.
Taking logarithmic derivatives gives
\[
\frac{B'(x)}{B(x)}
=
\ln 4
+2\psi(x+1)
-2\psi(2x+1/2),
\]
where $\psi(z):=(\ln\Gamma(z))'=\frac{\Gamma'(z)}{\Gamma(z)}$.
Followed by \cite[Formula 5.4.12, 5.4.13]{DLMF}, we have $\psi(1)=-\gamma$ and $\psi(1/2)=-\gamma-2\ln 2$, where $\gamma$ is the Euler constant. Then
\[
B'(0)=[\ln 4+2\psi(1)-2\psi(1/2)]B(0)=6\ln 2.
\]
Therefore,
\[
B(x)=1+6x\ln 2+O(x^2)\qquad (x\to0^+),
\]
and consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lhs 3log2}
  \frac{4^x\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(x)\Gamma(x+1)}
{\Gamma(2x+1/2)}
=
\frac1x+6\ln 2+O(x)
\qquad (x\to0^+).
\end{equation}

Comparing \eqref{eq:rhs 3log2} and \eqref{eq:lhs 3log2}, the formula
\[
3\ln 2=2+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
 \frac{6n+1}{2n(2n+1)}\binom{2n}{n}^{\!2}\frac1{64^n}.
\]
holds. This finishes the proof.
head: environment

label: lem:Unk rep
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Unk rep}
  $U(n,k)$ has an equivalent representation:
  \[
  U(n,k)=4^{-n-k}\frac{\Gamma(n+1/2)\Gamma(n+2k+1/2)}{\pi\,\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(n+k+1)\Gamma(k+1)}.\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
From the definition
\[
U(n,k)=4^{-n}\frac{(1/2)_n(1/2+2k)_n}{(1)_n(1+k)_n}
\frac{(1/4)_k(3/4)_k}{(1)_k^2},
\]
and the identity $(a)_m=\Gamma(a+m)/\Gamma(a)$, we obtain
\[
U(n,k)=
4^{-n}
\frac{\Gamma(n+1/2)\Gamma(n+2k+1/2)}{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(n+k+1)\Gamma(k+1)}
R_k,
\]
where
\[
R_k=
\frac{\Gamma(k+1/4)\Gamma(k+3/4)}{\Gamma(1/2)\Gamma(2k+1/2)
 \Gamma(1/4)\Gamma(3/4)}.
\]

By Legendre's duplication formula (see \cite[Formula 5.5.5]{DLMF}), $\Gamma(z)\Gamma\left(z+\frac12\right)=2^{1-2z}\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(2z)$. Let $z=k+\frac14$, we have
\[
\Gamma\left(k+\frac14\right)
\Gamma\left(k+\frac34\right)=
2^{1/2-2k}\sqrt{\pi}
\Gamma\left(2k+\frac12\right).
\]
Moreover, since $\Gamma\left(\frac12\right)=\sqrt{\pi}$ and $\Gamma\left(\frac14\right)
\Gamma\left(\frac34\right)=
\frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi/4)}=
\pi\sqrt{2}$,
\[
R_k=\frac{4^{-k}}{\pi}.
\]
Substituting this into the preceding expression yields
\[
U(n,k)
=
4^{-n-k}
\frac{\Gamma(n+1/2)\Gamma(n+2k+1/2)}
{\pi\,\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(n+k+1)\Gamma(k+1)},
\]
as required.
head: environment

label: coro:U(n+1/2,k)
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the preceding lemma,
\[
U\left(n+\frac12,k\right)=
4^{-n-k-1/2}
\frac{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(n+2k+1)}{\pi\,\Gamma(n+3/2)\Gamma(n+k+3/2)\Gamma(k+1)}.
\]
Using $(a)_n=\Gamma(a+n)/\Gamma(a)$, we obtain
\[
U\left(n+\frac12,k\right)=
4^{-n-k-1/2}
\frac{\Gamma(2k+1)}{\pi\,\Gamma(3/2)\Gamma(k+3/2)\Gamma(k+1)}
\frac{(1)_n(1+2k)_n}{(3/2)_n(k+3/2)_n}.
\]
Since $\Gamma\left(\frac32\right)=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}$ and Legendre's duplication formula (see \cite[Formula 5.5.5]{DLMF}), applied with $z=k+1$, we have:
\[
\Gamma(k+1)\Gamma\left(k+\frac32\right)=
2^{-2k-1}\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(2k+2)=2^{-2k-1}(2k+1)\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(2k+1).
\]
Then
\[
U\left(n+\frac12,k\right)=
\frac{2}{\pi^2(2k+1)}\,4^{-n}
\frac{(1)_n(1+2k)_n}
     {(3/2)_n(k+3/2)_n},
\]
as claimed.

label: thm:zeta3
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: eq:k sum
title: Proof
body_md:
We use the WZ pair in \eqref{eq:kernel}, \eqref{eq:pair} and shift the WZ identity \eqref{eq:wz} by $n\mapsto n+\frac12$ and $k\mapsto k+y, y\ge 0$. Summing the equation over $n\ge 0$ and using the fact $\lim_{n\to\infty}
F\left(n+\frac12,k+y\right)=0$, we have
\[
F\left(\frac12,k+y\right)
=
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
G\left(n+\frac12,k+y\right)-\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
G\left(n+\frac12,k+y+1\right).
\]
Sum both sides of the equation from $k=0$ to $k=\infty$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:k sum}
  \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
F\left(\frac12,k+y\right)
=
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
G\left(n+\frac12,y\right)-\lim_{k\to\infty}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
G\left(n+\frac12,k+y\right).
\end{equation}



We first verify the limit of the summation of $G(n+\frac12,k+y)$ as $k\to\infty$. By Corollary \ref{coro:U(n+1/2,k)},
\[
U\left(n+\frac12,k\right)
=
\frac{2}{\pi^2(2k+1)}\,4^{-n}
\frac{(1)_n(1+2k)_n}
     {(3/2)_n(k+3/2)_n}.
\]
Since
\[
\frac{(1+2k)_n}{(k+3/2)_n}=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{2k+1+j}{k+3/2+j} \le 2^n\quad \mathrm{and}\quad \frac{(1)_n}{(3/2)_n}\le 1,
\]
we have
\[
0<
U\left(n+\frac12,k\right)
\le
\frac{2}{\pi^2(2k+1)}2^{-n}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
G\left(n+\frac12,k\right)
=
U\left(n+\frac12,k\right)
\frac{k(3n+2k+2)}
     {2(n+k+1/2)(n+1)}.
\]
Since
\[
\frac{3n+2k+2}{n+k+1/2}\le 4,
\]
it follows that
\[
0\le
G\left(n+\frac12,k\right)
\le
\frac{2}{\pi^2}
\frac{2^{-n}}{n+1}.
\]
Thus $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
G\left(n+\frac12,k\right)$ converges uniformly for $k\ge 0$. For each fixed $n$, the limit of
$G(n+\frac12,k)$ as $k\to\infty$ exists. Hence, by the above
summable majorant and dominated convergence, denote
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
G\left(n+\frac12,k\right)\longrightarrow L
\qquad (k\to\infty)
\]
for some finite constant $L$.

Now followed by the equation \eqref{eq:k sum} and $L$ is independent of $y$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq: sum k+y}
  \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
F\left(\frac12,k+y\right)
=
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
G\left(n+\frac12,y\right)-L.
\end{equation}
At $y=0$, the explicit factor $k$ in $G(n+1/2,k)$ gives $G\left(n+\frac12,0\right)=0$ and hence the summation is zero. Therefore, subtracting the identity
\eqref{eq: sum k+y} at $y=0$ from \eqref{eq: sum k+y}, we have
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\left[
F\left(\frac12,k+y\right)
-
F\left(\frac12,k\right)
\right]
=
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
G\left(n+\frac12,y\right).
\]
Dividing by $y>0$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq: differential y}
  \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\frac{
F(1/2,k+y)-F(1/2,k)
}{y}
=
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
\frac{G(n+1/2,y)}{y}.
\end{equation}

We next justify taking the limit $y\to0^+$ in \eqref{eq: differential y}, by Corollary \ref{coro:U(n+1/2,k)},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:derivative F(1/2,k)}
 U\left(\frac12,k\right)
=
\frac{2}{\pi^2(2k+1)}\qquad F\left(\frac12,k\right)
=
-\frac{1}{\pi^2(2k+1)^2}\quad\mathrm{and}\quad \partial_k F(\frac{1}{2},k)=\frac{4}{\pi^2(2k+1)^3}. 
\end{equation}
Then the mean value theorem implies, for $0<y\le1$,
\[
\left|
\frac{F(1/2,k+y)-F(1/2,k)}{y}
\right|
\le
\frac{4}{\pi^2(2k+1)^3}.
\]
The majorant on the right is summable.

On the other hand,
\[
\frac{G(n+1/2,y)}{y}
=
U\left(n+\frac12,y\right)
\frac{3n+2y+2}
{2(n+y+1/2)(n+1)}.
\]
Using the estimates obtained above,
\[
U\left(n+\frac12,y\right)
\le
\frac{2}{\pi^2(2y+1)}2^{-n}
\le
\frac{2}{\pi^2}2^{-n},\qquad\frac{3n+2y+2}{n+y+1/2}\le4,
\]
we obtain
\[
0\le
\frac{G(n+1/2,y)}{y}
\le
\frac{4}{\pi^2}
\frac{2^{-n}}{n+1}.
\]
Again, the majorant is summable. Therefore, by dominated convergence,
letting $y\to0^+$ in \eqref{eq: differential y} yields
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\partial_kF\left(\frac12,k\right)
=
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
\partial_kG\left(n+\frac12,0\right).
\]

For the left-hand side, we have:
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\partial_kF\left(\frac12,k\right)=
\frac{4}{\pi^2}
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(2k+1)^3} =
\frac{4}{\pi^2}
\left(1-\frac{1}{2^3}\right)\zeta(3) =
\frac{7\zeta(3)}{2\pi^2}.
\]
For the right-hand side, the explicit factor $k$ gives:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:derivative G(n+1/2,0)}
  \partial_kG\left(n+\frac12,0\right)=
U\left(n+\frac12,0\right)
\frac{3n+2}{(2n+1)(n+1)}
\end{equation}
and Corollary \ref{coro:U(n+1/2,k)} gives
\[
U\left(n+\frac12,0\right)=
\frac{2}{\pi^2}4^{-n}
\frac{(1)_n^2}{(3/2)_n^2}=
\frac{2\cdot4^n}{\pi^2(2n+1)^2\binom{2n}{n}^2}
\]

Therefore
\[
\frac{7\zeta(3)}{2\pi^2}=
\frac{2}{\pi^2}
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
\frac{(3n+2)4^n}{(2n+1)^3(n+1)\binom{2n}{n}^2}
\]
i.e.,
\[
\zeta(3)=
\frac{4}{7}
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
\frac{(3n+2)4^n}{(2n+1)^3(n+1)\binom{2n}{n}^2},
\]
which proves the theorem.

title: Remark
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The upper-truncation congruence in \eqref{eq:2log2-upper} is stronger than what is implied by the divisibility of the individual summands. It is also worth noting that the full truncation behaves quite
differently. If denoting
\[
S:=
\sum_{n=1}^{p-1}
\frac{4n+1}{2n(2n+1)}
\binom{2n}{n}^{2}\frac{1}{2^{4n}},
\]
then
\[
v_p\bigl(S\bigr)=-1.
\]
Indeed, if
\[
a_n=
\frac{4n+1}{2n(2n+1)}
\binom{2n}{n}^{2}\frac{1}{2^{4n}},
\]
then \(a_n\in\mathbb Z_p\) for
\(n\neq (p-1)/2\), whereas
\[
v_p\left(a_{(p-1)/2}\right)=-1.
\]
Consequently, the middle term is the unique term of negative
\(p\)-adic valuation in the full truncation, which further explains
the natural separation into the lower, middle, and upper ranges.

label: eq:N-wz-sum
title: Proof
body_md:
Summing the WZ relation $F(n+1,x)-F(n,x)=G(n,x+1)-G(n,x)$ over $0\leq n\leq N$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:N-wz-sum}
F(N+1,x)=
\sum_{n=0}^{N}G(n,x+1)
-\sum_{n=0}^{N}G(n,x).
\end{equation}
By the definition of $H(n,x)$, we have
\[
G(n,x)=\frac{x}{2}
\frac{(1/4)_x(3/4)_x}{(1)_x^2}H(n,x).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\frac{
(1/4)_{x+1}(3/4)_{x+1}/(1)_{x+1}^2
}{(1/4)_x(3/4)_x/(1)_x^2}=
\frac{(4x+1)(4x+3)}{16(x+1)^2}.
\]
Substituting these expressions into
\eqref{eq:N-wz-sum} and cancelling the common
factor yields
\begin{equation}
\frac{(4x+1)(4x+3)}{16(x+1)}
\sum_{n=0}^{N}H(n,x+1)
-x\sum_{n=0}^{N}H(n,x)=-\frac{N+1}{N+1+x}4^{-(N+1)}
\frac{(1/2)_{N+1}(1/2+2x)_{N+1}}
{(1)_{N+1}(1+x)_{N+1}}.
\label{eq:N-wz-identity}
\end{equation}
This identity is initially obtained for generic $x$ and
extends as a rational identity wherever the displayed
expressions are defined.

Now set
\[
x_N=-\frac{2N+1}{4}.
\]
Since$\left(\frac12+2x_N\right)_{N+1}=(-N)_{N+1}=0$,
the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:N-wz-identity}
vanishes.

Now we prove $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^N H(n,x_N)=0$ by induction. For $N=0,1$, the coefficient
$(4x_N+1)(4x_N+3)$ also vanishes. Since $x_N\neq0$,
we immediately obtain
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{N}H(n,x_N)=0\quad(N=0,1).
\]
For $N\geq2$, assuming that the identity holds for $N-2$, observe that
\[
x_N+1=x_{N-2},
\qquad
\frac12+2(x_N+1)=-(N-2).
\]
Because the term $(1/2+2(x_N+1))_n$ appears in $H(n,x_N+1)$, $H(n,x_N+1)=0$ for $n\geq N-1$. Then
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{N}H(n,x_N+1)
=
\sum_{n=0}^{N-2}H(n,x_{N-2}).
\]
By the induction hypothesis, the latter sum vanishes. Substituting into
\eqref{eq:N-wz-identity} gives
\[
x_N\sum_{n=0}^{N}H(n,x_N)=0.
\]
Since $x_N\neq0$, the desired identity follows.
